The big picture

The limit of a function \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = a describes the values f(x) for x near x_0, never at x_0: the value f(x_0) may differ from a or not exist at all. It is made precise in two equivalent ways: the \varepsilon–\delta definition (every output tolerance \varepsilon can be met by some input tolerance \delta on a punctured neighbourhood, around an accumulation point of the domain), and Heine's (sequential) definition, which reduces function limits to the sequence limits of 7 Limits of Sequences: f(x_n) \to a for every sequence x_n \to x_0, x_n \neq x_0. Heine's form also gives the standard proof that a limit does not exist: two approaching sequences with different image limits (as for \sin(1/x)). With the definitions in place, the toolbox of chapter 7 carries over: limit laws, direct substitution for polynomials and rational functions, cancelling a 0/0 factor, order preservation, the squeeze theorem, and the Cauchy criterion. The point x_0 may be replaced by \pm\infty (limits at infinity, horizontal asymptotes, comparing degrees), the value a by \pm\infty (infinite limits, vertical asymptotes), and the approach may come from one side only (one-sided limits): a two-sided limit exists iff both one-sided limits exist and agree. Infinitesimal functions (\alpha(x) \to 0) give the useful form f = a + \alpha, and monotonic functions always have one-sided limits at the ends of their domain. Two special limits, \frac{\sin x}{x} \to 1 and \left(1 + \frac1x\right)^x \to e, generate a whole family of trigonometric and exponential limits.

Limits in robotics and AI

What happens when a change in the input becomes very small?

Robotics: velocity at an instant. If s(t) is a robot's position, the average velocity over a short time interval h is

v_h = \frac{s(t+h) - s(t)}{h}.

What happens as h \to 0?

AI: sensitivity of a loss. If J(w) is the training loss depending on a model parameter w, compare

\frac{J(w+h) - J(w)}{h}.

What happens as h \to 0?

Symbols
  • s(t) — position of the robot (m) at time t (s); h — a short time step (s), h \neq 0
  • v_h — the average velocity (m/s) over the interval from t to t + h
  • J(w) — the training loss (dimensionless) as a function of one model parameter w; h — a small change of the parameter
  • \frac{J(w+h) - J(w)}{h} — the change in loss per unit change of the parameter

Both questions lead to limits. Later, we will use them to define derivatives.

Intuition — why we cannot just "plug in h = 0"

At h = 0 both quotients become \frac{0}{0}, which is meaningless. Yet for small h they settle near a definite number (the instantaneous velocity, the slope of the loss). A function limit is exactly the tool for "the value a formula approaches as h \to 0, although the formula is undefined at h = 0". That is why the whole lecture insists on near x_0, not at x_0.

What does a limit describe?

A limit describes the values f(x) as x gets close to a given point x_0, without requiring x = x_0.

Picture on the slide: a straight line through the point (1, 2) with an open circle at x = 1 (labelled "limit 2") and a separate orange dot for f(1) above the line.

\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2.

Here f(1) can be different from 2. It may even be undefined. The value at the point and the limit at the point are different notions.

Symbols
  • \lim_{x \to 1} f(x) — "the limit of f(x) as x tends to 1": the number the values f(x) approach when x comes close to 1 with x \neq 1
  • f(1) — the value of the function at the point 1 itself (irrelevant for the limit)

The ε–δ picture

We choose a tolerance \varepsilon > 0 for the output.

The blue band is the output tolerance (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon); the orange strip is the input window (x_0 - \delta, x_0 + \delta). For every x in the strip (except x_0) the graph stays inside the band.

Find \delta > 0 so that, whenever x is sufficiently close to x_0, the value f(x) lies in the blue band:

0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta \implies \lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • a — the (candidate) limit; x_0 — the point x approaches
  • \varepsilon > 0 — the output tolerance (how close f(x) must be to a), chosen first, by "the opponent"
  • \delta > 0 — the input tolerance (how close x must be to x_0), which we must find for the given \varepsilon
  • 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert — x \neq x_0: the point itself is excluded

Interactive version: Desmos: try it (linked on slide 4).

Connection

This is the \varepsilon–N game of 7 Limits of Sequences › Definition of convergence with one change: there, "late enough" meant n \ge N; here, "close enough" means 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta. The output side, \lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon, is the same \varepsilon-neighbourhood as before (3 Set of Real Numbers › Neighbourhoods).

Definition of the limit of a function

Let f : D \to \mathbb{R}, D \subseteq \mathbb{R}, and let x_0 be an accumulation point of D.

We write \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = a if

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0\ \forall x \in D : \quad 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta \implies \lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • D \subseteq \mathbb{R} — the domain of f; x \in D — only points where f is defined are tested
  • x_0 — an accumulation point of D (it need not belong to D); a \in \mathbb{R} — the limit
  • \varepsilon, \delta — output and input tolerances, as in the picture above
  • \forall "for all", \exists "there exists" (1 Elements of Logic); the order \forall\varepsilon\ \exists\delta means \delta is chosen after \varepsilon
  • The number \delta may depend on \varepsilon.
  • The condition 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert excludes the point x_0.
  • f(x_0) need not exist, and need not equal a.
Intuition — what an accumulation point of D is

x_0 is an accumulation point of the set D if every punctured neighbourhood of x_0 contains at least one point of D: formally, \forall r > 0\ \exists x \in D : 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < r. Equivalently, there is a sequence in D \setminus \{x_0\} converging to x_0. Examples: 1 is an accumulation point of \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\} and of (0, 1), although it is in neither set. An isolated point, such as 5 in D = (0,1) \cup \{5\}, is not. The condition is needed so that "x close to x_0" is possible at all; at an isolated point every a would satisfy the definition vacuously.

Worked example — an \varepsilon–\delta proof with a non-linear function

Show \lim_{x \to 2} x^2 = 4.

  1. Rewrite the distance to the limit: \lvert x^2 - 4\rvert = \lvert x - 2\rvert \cdot \lvert x + 2\rvert. The first factor we control with \delta; the second must be bounded.
  2. Bound the extra factor by restricting \delta \le 1: if \lvert x - 2\rvert < 1, then 1 < x < 3, so \lvert x + 2\rvert < 5.
  3. Choose \delta: \delta = \min\{1, \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\}.
  4. Check: if 0 < \lvert x - 2\rvert < \delta, then \lvert x^2 - 4\rvert < 5\lvert x - 2\rvert < 5 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{5} = \varepsilon. Pattern: factor out \lvert x - x_0\rvert, bound what is left on a fixed small window, take \delta as the minimum of the window size and \varepsilon / \text{bound}. (Checked numerically for random \varepsilon and x.)

A limit at a point where the function is undefined

Example: f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}, defined on \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\}. Find \lim_{x \to 1} f(x). For x \neq 1,

f(x) = \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x - 1} = x + 1.

Choose \varepsilon > 0 and set \delta = \varepsilon. If 0 < \lvert x - 1\rvert < \delta, then

\lvert f(x) - 2\rvert = \lvert x + 1 - 2\rvert = \lvert x - 1\rvert < \delta = \varepsilon.

Hence

\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} = 2,

although f(1) is undefined.

Symbols
  • \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\} — all reals except 1 (where the denominator vanishes)
  • \delta = \varepsilon — works here because \lvert f(x) - 2\rvert equals \lvert x - 1\rvert exactly
Why may we cancel x - 1, if f is not defined at 1?

Cancelling is allowed for every x \neq 1, because there x - 1 \neq 0. And x \neq 1 is the only case the definition ever looks at (0 < \lvert x - 1\rvert). So f and x + 1 agree on the whole punctured neighbourhood, and functions that agree there have the same limit. The cancelled form x + 1 is not the same function as f (it is also defined at 1), but it has the same limit at 1.

Quick check: a limit at a missing point

Question: Consider

f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}, \qquad x \neq 2.

Find \lim_{x \to 2} f(x). Does f(2) exist?

For x \neq 2,

f(x) = \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x - 2} = x + 2.

Thus \lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 4, although f(2) is undefined.

Symbols
  • x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) — difference of squares; the factor x - 2 cancels for x \neq 2

More questions: Khan Academy – limits by factoring / using algebra (linked on slide 7).

The value at x_0 does not determine the limit

Consider the following functions near x_0 = 1.

Three functions that coincide with the same line for x \neq 1: f(1) undefined (hole), g(1) = 3 (a dot off the line), h(1) = 2 (the dot on the line).

All three functions have the same limit:

\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = \lim_{x \to 1} h(x) = 2.
Symbols
  • f, g, h — three functions equal to each other for every x \neq 1, differing only at x = 1

Practice: Khan Academy – two-sided limits from graphs (linked on slide 8).

Common mistake — "the limit is just the value at the point"

Tempting, because for polynomials and most "nice" functions the two coincide (see Polynomial and rational functions). But the definition never looks at x_0: g above has g(1) = 3 and limit 2. The case limit = value is special and gets its own name next lecture: continuity. So never answer "\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = f(x_0)" without a reason (a theorem such as direct substitution, or an \varepsilon–\delta check).

Punctured neighbourhoods

For r > 0, a punctured neighbourhood of x_0 is

\dot U(x_0, r) = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < r\}.

Picture on the slide: the interval from x_0 - r to x_0 + r on the number line, with an open circle at x_0.

\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = a \iff \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0 : \quad f\big(D \cap \dot U(x_0, \delta)\big) \subset U(a, \varepsilon).

Here U(a, \varepsilon) = (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon); the puncture excludes x_0, even when f(x_0) is defined.

Symbols
  • \dot U(x_0, r) = (x_0 - r, x_0) \cup (x_0, x_0 + r) — the open interval of radius r around x_0 with x_0 removed (the dot marks the puncture)
  • U(a, \varepsilon) — the ordinary \varepsilon-neighbourhood of a (3 Set of Real Numbers › Neighbourhoods)
  • f(D \cap \dot U(x_0, \delta)) — the image set: all values f(x) for x in the domain and in the punctured \delta-neighbourhood
  • \subset — "is contained in"
Intuition

This is the same definition, written with sets instead of inequalities: "0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta, x \in D" is "x \in D \cap \dot U(x_0, \delta)", and "\lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon" is "f(x) \in U(a, \varepsilon)". In words: every target window around a catches the image of some punctured window around x_0.

Heine's definition in terms of sequences

Let x_0 \in \mathbb{R}, D \subseteq \mathbb{R}, f : D \to \mathbb{R}. We say that

\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = a

if and only if every sequence (x_n) with

x_n \in D \setminus \{x_0\}, \qquad x_n \to x_0

satisfies f(x_n) \to a.

Symbols
  • (x_n) — a sequence of inputs in the domain, never equal to x_0, converging to x_0 (in the sense of 7 Limits of Sequences › Definition of convergence)
  • f(x_n) — the image sequence: the outputs along that approach; f(x_n) \to a is again a sequence limit

A function has the same limit along every possible approach to x_0.

Unclear (slide 10)

Unlike slide 5, Heine's definition on slide 10 does not repeat that x_0 must be an accumulation point of D. Without that assumption there may be no sequence x_n \in D \setminus \{x_0\} with x_n \to x_0 at all, and then "every sequence satisfies f(x_n) \to a" holds vacuously for every a. The equivalence with the \varepsilon–\delta definition (Key facts, slide 60) is meant under the same assumption as slide 5.

Why are the \varepsilon–\delta definition and Heine's definition equivalent?

\varepsilon–\delta ⇒ Heine. Let x_n \to x_0, x_n \in D \setminus \{x_0\}, and let \varepsilon > 0. Take the \delta from the definition. Since x_n \to x_0, there is N with \lvert x_n - x_0\rvert < \delta for n \ge N; also x_n \neq x_0. So \lvert f(x_n) - a\rvert < \varepsilon for n \ge N: f(x_n) \to a. Heine ⇒ \varepsilon–\delta (by contrapositive, 1 Elements of Logic). Suppose the \varepsilon–\delta condition fails: there is \varepsilon_0 > 0 such that for every \delta some x \in D has 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta but \lvert f(x) - a\rvert \ge \varepsilon_0. Use \delta = \frac1n for n = 1, 2, \dots and call that point x_n. Then x_n \to x_0, x_n \neq x_0, but \lvert f(x_n) - a\rvert \ge \varepsilon_0 for all n, so f(x_n) \not\to a: Heine's condition fails too.

Using sequences to calculate a function limit

Example: Prove that \lim_{x \to 0} x^2 = 0 by Heine's criterion. Take any sequence (x_n) with x_n \neq 0 and x_n \to 0. By the arithmetic rules for sequences,

\lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n^2 = \left(\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n\right)^2 = 0.

Since this holds for every sequence approaching 0 (but not equal to 0), \lim_{x \to 0} x^2 = 0.

Symbols
  • f(x) = x^2; x_n^2 = x_n \cdot x_n, whose limit is the product of the limits (7 Limits of Sequences › Arithmetic of finite limits)
Common mistake — testing one sequence and concluding the limit exists

Heine's criterion needs every sequence. Checking x_n = \frac1n alone proves nothing: for f(x) = \sin(1/x) the sequence x_n = \frac{1}{n\pi} gives f(x_n) = 0 \to 0, yet the limit does not exist (below). One sequence (or one table of values) can only disprove a candidate; to prove a limit, argue for an arbitrary sequence, as the slide does, or use \varepsilon–\delta or the limit laws.

When does a function have no limit?

There are two useful ways to demonstrate non-existence.

By the \varepsilon–\delta definition: For every candidate a \in \mathbb{R}, find \varepsilon_0 > 0 such that for every \delta > 0 there is x \in D with

0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta, \qquad \lvert f(x) - a\rvert \ge \varepsilon_0.

By Heine's criterion: Find two sequences x_n, y_n \in D \setminus \{x_0\} converging to x_0 for which f(x_n) and f(y_n) have different limits.

For a counterexample, two different approaches are enough.

Symbols
  • \varepsilon_0 — one fixed tolerance that can never be met, however small \delta is
  • (x_n), (y_n) — two approaches to x_0 from inside the domain, avoiding x_0
Intuition

The first method is the logical negation of the definition (1 Elements of Logic): \forall\varepsilon\ \exists\delta\ \forall x turns into \exists\varepsilon_0\ \forall\delta\ \exists x, and it must be done for every candidate a. The second method avoids the "every candidate" part: if a limit a existed, both image sequences would have to tend to a, so two different image limits rule out every a at once. (A single sequence whose image sequence diverges works just as well.)

An oscillating function: \sin(1/x)

Graph of \sin(1/x) on [-0.5, 0.5]: the oscillations get faster and faster as x \to 0, always between -1 and 1.

f(x) = \sin\frac1x, \qquad x \neq 0.

As x \to 0, the function oscillates between -1 and 1. The function does not have a limit at 0. We can prove this using two sequences.

Symbols
  • \frac1x — the argument of the sine (in radians); as x \to 0^+ it runs through (0, \infty), so the sine makes infinitely many full oscillations

Proving non-existence with two sequences

Example: f(x) = \sin(1/x) near x_0 = 0. Take

x_n = \frac{1}{n\pi}, \qquad y_n = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/2}, \qquad n \in \mathbb{N}.

Both satisfy x_n \to 0, y_n \to 0, and neither equals 0. But

f(x_n) = \sin(n\pi) = 0, \qquad f(y_n) = \sin\left(2\pi n + \pi/2\right) = 1.
Symbols
  • x_n — chosen so that \frac{1}{x_n} = n\pi, a zero of the sine
  • y_n — chosen so that \frac{1}{y_n} = 2\pi n + \frac\pi2, where the sine equals 1 (a maximum, shifted by full periods 2\pi n)

The two image sequences have different limits: 0 \neq 1. Therefore \lim_{x \to 0} \sin(1/x) does not exist.

Intuition — how to find such sequences

Work backwards from the outputs you want: pick two values the function keeps taking (here 0 and 1), solve \sin(1/x) = 0 and \sin(1/x) = 1 for x, and list the solutions closer and closer to x_0. The same recipe shows that \cos(1/x) has no limit at 0 (x_n = \frac{1}{2\pi n} gives 1, y_n = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi} gives -1). Contrast: x \sin(1/x) \to 0, because the factor x damps the oscillation (Operations with infinitesimal functions).

Proving non-existence by the ε–δ definition

Assume, for contradiction, that

\lim_{x \to 0} \sin\frac1x = a

for some a \in \mathbb{R}. Choose \varepsilon = \frac12. Then there exists \delta > 0 such that

0 < \lvert x\rvert < \delta \implies \left\lvert \sin\frac1x - a \right\rvert < \frac12.

Now choose n \in \mathbb{N} so large that

x_1 = \frac{1}{\frac\pi2 + 2\pi n} < \delta, \qquad x_2 = \frac{1}{\frac{3\pi}{2} + 2\pi n} < \delta.

Then 0 < x_1, x_2 < \delta and \sin\frac{1}{x_1} = 1, \sin\frac{1}{x_2} = -1. Hence \lvert 1 - a\rvert < \frac12, \lvert -1 - a\rvert < \frac12. But then

2 = \lvert 1 - (-1)\rvert \le \lvert 1 - a\rvert + \lvert -1 - a\rvert < \frac12 + \frac12 = 1,

a contradiction.

Symbols
  • a — any candidate limit; \varepsilon = \frac12 — the tolerance that will fail
  • x_1, x_2 — two points closer than \delta to 0 where the sine is +1 and -1
  • the step "\le" is the triangle inequality \lvert u - v\rvert \le \lvert u - a\rvert + \lvert a - v\rvert (3 Set of Real Numbers) with u = 1, v = -1
Intuition

The idea in one sentence: inside every window around 0 the function takes both values 1 and -1, which are 2 apart; no band of width 2\varepsilon = 1 around any a can contain both. Any \varepsilon \le 1 (half the gap) would do.

Limit laws

Sums and products

Suppose \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = A and \lim_{x \to x_0} g(x) = B, where A, B \in \mathbb{R}.

Sum and difference

\lim_{x \to x_0} (f \pm g)(x) = A \pm B.

Products

\lim_{x \to x_0} (fg)(x) = AB.

Constant multiples

\lim_{x \to x_0} c f(x) = cA \qquad (c \in \mathbb{R}).

Powers

\lim_{x \to x_0} (f(x))^n = A^n \qquad (n \in \mathbb{N}).
Symbols
  • A, B — the finite limits of f and g at x_0
  • (f \pm g)(x) = f(x) \pm g(x), (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x) — pointwise operations (5 Functions › Adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing — pointwise)
  • c — a fixed real constant; n — a fixed natural exponent

Quotients and roots

Suppose \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = A and \lim_{x \to x_0} g(x) = B.

Quotients: If B \neq 0,

\lim_{x \to x_0} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{A}{B}.

Roots: For an integer n \ge 2,

\lim_{x \to x_0} \sqrt[n]{f(x)} = \sqrt[n]{A},

provided the roots are real-valued near x_0 (for even n, f(x) \ge 0 and A \ge 0).

Symbols
  • B \neq 0 — the limit of the denominator must be non-zero (then g(x) \neq 0 near x_0 as well, so the quotient is defined there)
  • \sqrt[n]{\ \cdot\ } — the real n-th root (3 Set of Real Numbers › Roots and rational powers)

When the denominator tends to 0, the quotient law cannot be applied directly.

Why do the limit laws hold?

Through Heine's definition they are the sequence laws in disguise. Take any x_n \to x_0, x_n \neq x_0, in the domain. Then f(x_n) \to A and g(x_n) \to B, so by 7 Limits of Sequences › Arithmetic of finite limits f(x_n) + g(x_n) \to A + B, f(x_n)g(x_n) \to AB, and \frac{f(x_n)}{g(x_n)} \to \frac AB if B \neq 0. Since this holds for every such sequence, Heine gives the function law. This is the main payoff of Heine's definition: every theorem about sequence limits becomes a theorem about function limits for free.

Polynomial and rational functions

Polynomial: For P(x) = c_m x^m + \dots + c_1 x + c_0,

\lim_{x \to x_0} P(x) = P(x_0).

Rational function: If Q(x_0) \neq 0,

\lim_{x \to x_0} \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = \frac{P(x_0)}{Q(x_0)}.
Symbols
  • c_0, \dots, c_m — real coefficients; m — the degree of P
  • P, Q — polynomials; \frac{P}{Q} — a rational function (5 Functions › Rational functions)
  • Q(x_0) \neq 0 — the denominator does not vanish at the point

This is why direct substitution works for so many elementary limits.

Why does substitution work for polynomials?

\lim_{x \to x_0} x = x_0 (take \delta = \varepsilon) and \lim_{x \to x_0} c = c. A polynomial is built from x and constants by finitely many products and sums, so the power, constant-multiple and sum laws give \lim P(x) = c_m x_0^m + \dots + c_0 = P(x_0). For \frac PQ, add the quotient law, which needs exactly Q(x_0) \neq 0.

Direct substitution

  1. \displaystyle\lim_{x \to c} (x^3 + 4x^2 - 3) = c^3 + 4c^2 - 3.
  2. \displaystyle\lim_{x \to c} \frac{x^4 + x^2 - 1}{x^2 + 5} = \frac{c^4 + c^2 - 1}{c^2 + 5}.
  3. \displaystyle\lim_{x \to -2} \sqrt{4x^2 - 3} = \sqrt{4(-2)^2 - 3} = \sqrt{13}.

All three follow from the limit laws and the continuity of the operations involved.

Intuition

In (2) the denominator c^2 + 5 \ge 5 is never 0, so the rational rule applies at every c. In (3) the radicand 4x^2 - 3 is 13 > 0 at x = -2, so it stays positive nearby and the root law applies. Substitution is legal exactly when every law used along the way has its hypothesis satisfied.

When direct substitution gives 0/0

Example: \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x^2 - x}. Direct substitution gives 0/0: the quotient rule does not apply yet.

For x \neq 1,

\frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x^2 - x} = \frac{(x-1)(x+2)}{x(x-1)} = \frac{x+2}{x}.

Now the denominator has a nonzero limit:

\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x^2 - x} = \frac{1+2}{1} = 3.
Symbols
  • 0/0 — numerator and denominator both tend to 0: an indeterminate form, not a value
  • (x - 1) — the common factor; it exists because 1 is a root of both polynomials

Practice: Khan Academy – limits using algebra (linked on slide 20).

Worked example — two ways to remove a 0/0

(a) Factor. \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 - 2x - 3}.

  1. Substitute first: \frac{0}{0}, so a factor (x - 3) hides in both.
  2. Factor: x^2 - 9 = (x-3)(x+3), x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x-3)(x+1).
  3. Cancel for x \neq 3 and substitute: \frac{x+3}{x+1} \to \frac{6}{4} = \frac32.

(b) Rationalise (roots). \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{1+x} - 1}{x}.

  1. Substitute first: \frac00; no polynomial factor to cancel.
  2. Multiply by the conjugate \sqrt{1+x} + 1: numerator becomes (1 + x) - 1 = x.
  3. Cancel x \neq 0: \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x} + 1} \to \frac{1}{2}. (Both checked numerically.)
Common mistake — "0/0 = 0", "0/0 = 1" or "the limit doesn't exist"

\frac00 after substitution only says the quotient law does not apply yet. The limit can be any number (\frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} \to 2, \frac{\sin(2x)}{5x} \to \frac25) or fail to exist (\frac{\lvert x\rvert}{x}). The same warning as 7 Limits of Sequences › Indeterminate forms are warnings: simplify first, then substitute.

Comparison of function limits

Order is preserved. Let f, g : D \to \mathbb{R}, and suppose f(x) \le g(x) for all x in some open interval containing x_0, except possibly at x = x_0 itself. If the finite limits exist, then

\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) \le \lim_{x \to x_0} g(x).
Symbols
  • "some open interval containing x_0" — the inequality only needs to hold near x_0 (in the domain), not everywhere

Be careful: f(x) < g(x) does not imply strict inequality of the limits.

0 < x^2 \quad (x \neq 0), \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} 0 = \lim_{x \to 0} x^2 = 0.
Connection

The function version of 7 Limits of Sequences › Passing inequalities to the limit, proved via Heine: along any x_n \to x_0, f(x_n) \le g(x_n), so the limits of the image sequences keep the order. Strict inequalities are lost in the limit for the same reason as \frac1n > 0 but \lim \frac1n = 0.

Sandwich (squeeze) theorem

Theorem. Let f, g, h : D \to \mathbb{R} be such that

g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)

for all x in some open interval containing x_0, except possibly at x = x_0 itself. If \lim_{x \to x_0} g(x) = \lim_{x \to x_0} h(x) = a, then \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = a.

Symbols
  • g — the lower bound function, h — the upper bound function, f — the function trapped between them
  • a — the common limit of g and h, which is then forced on f

Picture on the slide: the graph of f wiggling between an upper curve h and a lower curve g that touch at the level 1 at x_0 = 0.

Connection

Same theorem as 7 Limits of Sequences › The squeeze (sandwich) theorem, transferred by Heine. Note the important difference: the squeeze theorem also tells you that the limit of f exists, whereas the order rule above assumes it.

Squeezing trigonometric functions

Example 1: -\lvert x\rvert \le \sin x \le \lvert x\rvert for x near 0.

\lim_{x \to 0} (-\lvert x\rvert) = \lim_{x \to 0} \lvert x\rvert = 0 \implies \lim_{x \to 0} \sin x = 0.

Example 2: 0 \le 1 - \cos x \le \lvert x\rvert near 0.

\lim_{x \to 0} (1 - \cos x) = 0 \implies \lim_{x \to 0} \cos x = 1.

Example 3: If \lvert f(x)\rvert \to 0, then f(x) \to 0, since

-\lvert f(x)\rvert \le f(x) \le \lvert f(x)\rvert.
Symbols
  • x — an angle in radians; \lvert x\rvert — its absolute value (the arc length on the unit circle)
  • in Example 2, 1 - \cos x is squeezed between 0 and \lvert x\rvert, and then \cos x = 1 - (1 - \cos x) \to 1 - 0
Why is \lvert\sin x\rvert \le \lvert x\rvert and 1 - \cos x \le \lvert x\rvert?

On the unit circle, an arc of length \lvert x\rvert ends at the point (\cos x, \sin x). The vertical distance \lvert \sin x\rvert to the horizontal axis is at most the straight-line distance to (1, 0), which is at most the arc length \lvert x\rvert. The same chord bound gives the horizontal distance 1 - \cos x \le \lvert x\rvert. (In fact 1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2\frac x2 \le 2\left(\frac x2\right)^2 = \frac{x^2}{2}, which is even smaller near 0.)

Worked example — squeezing a damped oscillation

Find \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \sin\frac1x.

  1. Spot the trouble: \sin\frac1x has no limit at 0 (Proving non-existence with two sequences), so the product law cannot be used.
  2. Bound the bad factor: -1 \le \sin\frac1x \le 1, so multiplying by x^2 \ge 0 gives -x^2 \le x^2\sin\frac1x \le x^2 for x \neq 0.
  3. Squeeze: -x^2 \to 0 and x^2 \to 0, so the limit is 0.

Limits as x \to +\infty and x \to -\infty

The input need not approach a finite point.

As x \to +\infty: \lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = a means

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists M \in \mathbb{R} : \quad x \in D,\ x > M \implies \lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon.

As x \to -\infty: \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = a means

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists m \in \mathbb{R} : \quad x \in D,\ x < m \implies \lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon.

In each case, the domain must contain points arbitrarily far in the indicated direction.

Symbols
  • M — a threshold: beyond it (to the right), all values are within \varepsilon of a; it plays the role of \delta
  • m — the corresponding threshold to the left for x \to -\infty
  • "D contains points arbitrarily far" — D is unbounded above (resp. below), the analogue of "x_0 is an accumulation point"
Connection

\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = a is the sequence definition with the integer index n \ge N replaced by a real variable x > M. In particular, if \lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = a, then the sequence a_n = f(n) tends to a (the converse fails: \sin(\pi x) has no limit at +\infty, but \sin(\pi n) = 0).

A horizontal asymptote

Example: f(x) = 2 + \dfrac1x for x \neq 0.

Graph on the slide: the curve 2 + \frac1x for x > 0, falling from about 3 towards the dashed line y = 2.

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \left(2 + \frac1x\right) = 2. \qquad \text{Also} \qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} \left(2 + \frac1x\right) = 2.

The line y = 2 is a horizontal asymptote.

Symbols
  • y = 2 — a horizontal line that the graph approaches as x \to +\infty or x \to -\infty
Intuition

Definition used here: the line y = a is a horizontal asymptote of f if \lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = a or \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = a. The two sides can have different asymptotes (e.g. \frac{\lvert x\rvert}{x}: y = 1 on the right, y = -1 on the left). The graph may even cross its asymptote; only the behaviour far out matters.

Practice: Khan Academy – limits at infinity, graphical (linked on slide 25).

Two elementary limits at infinity

For any fixed c \in \mathbb{R},

\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} c = c, \qquad \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac1x = 0.

Why? Choose \varepsilon > 0. If \lvert x\rvert > 1/\varepsilon, then

\left\lvert \frac1x - 0 \right\rvert = \frac{1}{\lvert x\rvert} < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • c — a constant function; \pm\infty — the statement holds for both +\infty and -\infty
  • \lvert x\rvert > \frac1\varepsilon — so M = \frac1\varepsilon works for +\infty and m = -\frac1\varepsilon for -\infty

The ordinary limit laws remain valid at +\infty or -\infty, provided the limits involved are finite and the usual assumptions hold.

A rational function at infinity

Example: \displaystyle\lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac{x^2 + x + 1}{x^2 - 1}. Divide numerator and denominator by x^2:

\frac{x^2 + x + 1}{x^2 - 1} = \frac{1 + \frac1x + \frac{1}{x^2}}{1 - \frac{1}{x^2}}.

Since 1/x \to 0 and 1/x^2 \to 0,

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac{x^2 + x + 1}{x^2 - 1} = \frac{1 + 0 + 0}{1 - 0} = 1.
Symbols
  • x^2 — the highest power in the denominator: dividing by it turns every other term into something that tends to 0
  • \frac{1}{x^2} = \frac1x \cdot \frac1x \to 0 \cdot 0 by the product law

A rational function with equal numerator and denominator degrees approaches the ratio of leading coefficients.

Rational functions: compare the degrees

Let P(x) have degree n and leading coefficient a_n \neq 0, and let Q(x) have degree m and leading coefficient b_m \neq 0.

For f(x) = P(x)/Q(x), the behaviour at +\infty is determined by the leading terms:

f(x) \sim \frac{a_n}{b_m} x^{n-m}.
Symbols
  • n, m — the degrees of P and Q; a_n, b_m — their leading (highest-power) coefficients
  • \sim — "behaves like": the quotient of the two sides tends to 1 as x \to +\infty (the slide uses the symbol without defining it)
  • x^{n-m} — a power of x with exponent n - m (negative, zero or positive)
n < mn = mn > m
\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = 0\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = \frac{a_n}{b_m}f(x) \to \pm\infty, depending on the sign of a_n / b_m

For x \to -\infty, the parity of n - m also affects the sign in the last case.

Connection

The same rule appeared for sequences in 7 Limits of Sequences › Comparing polynomial degrees; the proof is the same "divide by the highest power of the denominator" trick as on the previous slide.

Quick check: a limit at infinity

Question: Evaluate

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac{5x^2 - 7}{2x^2 + 3}.

Divide numerator and denominator by x^2:

\frac{5x^2 - 7}{2x^2 + 3} = \frac{5 - 7/x^2}{2 + 3/x^2}.

Since 1/x^2 \to 0,

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac{5x^2 - 7}{2x^2 + 3} = \frac52.
Symbols
  • n = m = 2, a_n = 5, b_m = 2: the equal-degree case of the table

More questions: Khan Academy – limits at infinity where x is unbounded (linked on slide 29).

The sign at negative infinity matters

Odd degree difference

f(x) = \frac{x^3 + 1}{x^2 + 1} \sim x. \qquad \lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = +\infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = -\infty.

Even degree difference

g(x) = \frac{x^4 + 1}{x^2 + 1} \sim x^2. \qquad \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} g(x) = +\infty.

To determine the sign, inspect the leading coefficient and the parity of n - m.

Symbols
  • n - m = 1 (odd) for f, n - m = 2 (even) for g; leading-coefficient ratio \frac{a_n}{b_m} = 1 > 0 in both
  • x^{n-m} keeps its sign for x \to -\infty if n - m is even and flips it if n - m is odd
Worked example — reading off limits at \pm\infty

(a) \displaystyle\lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac{3x^3 - x}{1 - 2x^3}. Degrees: n = m = 3. Leading coefficients: 3 and -2. Result: -\frac32. (b) \displaystyle\lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac{2x + 1}{x^2 + 3}. Degrees: n = 1 < m = 2. Result: 0. (c) \displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{-2x^3}{x^2 + 1}. Behaves like -2x^{1}; n - m = 1 is odd, so as x \to -\infty, -2x \to +\infty. Result: +\infty. (All three checked numerically.)

Infinite limits near a finite point

We write \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = +\infty if

\forall K > 0\ \exists \delta > 0 : \quad x \in D,\ 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta \implies f(x) > K.

Similarly, \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = -\infty if

\forall K > 0\ \exists \delta > 0 : \quad 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta \implies f(x) < -K.

These are infinite limits, not convergence to a real number.

Symbols
  • K > 0 — an arbitrarily large bound, chosen first; it replaces the tolerance \varepsilon
  • \delta — the radius of the punctured neighbourhood on which f exceeds K (or stays below -K)
Unclear (slide 31)

The definition of \lim f(x) = -\infty omits "x \in D", which the +\infty line above it includes. It is meant in the same way: only points of the domain are tested. Omission only.

Common mistake — "the limit is \infty, so the limit exists"

\lim f(x) = +\infty describes how f fails to have a (finite) limit: the values grow beyond every bound. As for sequences (7 Limits of Sequences › Infinite limits), the function does not converge, and the limit laws for finite limits do not apply to it (\infty - \infty, 0 \cdot \infty are indeterminate).

Vertical asymptotes: two different behaviours

Left: f(x) = 1/x^2 goes up on both sides of 0. Right: g(x) = 1/x goes down on the left of 0 and up on the right.

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x^2} = +\infty. \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac1x = -\infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac1x = +\infty.
Symbols
  • x \to 0^- — x approaches 0 from the left (x < 0); x \to 0^+ — from the right (x > 0); defined in One-sided limits
Intuition

Definition used here: the line x = x_0 is a vertical asymptote of f if at least one one-sided limit at x_0 is +\infty or -\infty. For \frac{1}{x^2} both sides agree, so the two-sided limit is +\infty. For \frac1x the sides disagree, so \lim_{x \to 0} \frac1x does not exist, not even as \pm\infty; only \lvert 1/x\rvert \to +\infty.

Infinitesimal and infinitely large functions

A function \alpha is infinitesimal as x \to x_0 if

\lim_{x \to x_0} \alpha(x) = 0.

A function f is infinitely large in magnitude as x \to x_0 if

\lim_{x \to x_0} \lvert f(x)\rvert = +\infty.

For instance, \alpha(x) = x^2 is infinitesimal as x \to 0, while f(x) = 1/x is infinitely large in magnitude.

Symbols
  • \alpha — the usual letter for an infinitesimal function (not an angle here)
  • \lvert f(x)\rvert \to +\infty — the size grows without bound; the sign may differ on the two sides (as for \frac1x)
Connection

The function version of 7 Limits of Sequences › Infinitesimal sequences. "Infinitesimal" is always relative to the approach: x^2 is infinitesimal as x \to 0 but infinitely large as x \to \infty.

A limit as a constant plus an infinitesimal

A function f has the finite limit a at x_0 if and only if it can be written near x_0 as

f(x) = a + \alpha(x), \qquad \alpha(x) \to 0 \quad (x \to x_0).

Proof: Set \alpha(x) = f(x) - a. Then

\lim_{x \to x_0} \alpha(x) = \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) - a.

Thus \alpha(x) \to 0 exactly when f(x) \to a. It is enough that the identity holds on a punctured neighbourhood of x_0.

Symbols
  • a — the finite limit; \alpha(x) = f(x) - a — the error of replacing f(x) by a
Intuition

"Limit = main part + vanishing error." This is the form engineers use all the time: near x_0, f(x) \approx a with an error \alpha(x) that can be made as small as we like. Next lecture's derivatives refine it to "f(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0) + \text{smaller error}".

Operations with infinitesimal functions

Suppose \alpha(x) \to 0 and \beta(x) \to 0 as x \to x_0.

Sum

\alpha(x) + \beta(x) \to 0.

Product

\alpha(x)\beta(x) \to 0.

Bounded factor: If g is bounded near x_0, then

g(x)\alpha(x) \to 0.
Symbols
  • \alpha, \beta — two infinitesimal functions at the same x_0
  • "g bounded near x_0" — there are C > 0 and r > 0 with \lvert g(x)\rvert \le C for all x \in D \cap \dot U(x_0, r) (5 Functions › Bounded and unbounded functions); g need not have a limit

In general, an infinitesimal times an unbounded function need not be infinitesimal: x \cdot (1/x) = 1 for x \neq 0.

Why does a bounded factor not spoil an infinitesimal?

If \lvert g(x)\rvert \le C near x_0, then 0 \le \lvert g(x)\alpha(x)\rvert \le C\lvert\alpha(x)\rvert \to 0, so \lvert g\alpha\rvert \to 0 by the squeeze theorem, and then g\alpha \to 0 by Example 3 of Squeezing trigonometric functions. This is the quick way to settle x\sin\frac1x \to 0 as x \to 0 or \frac{\sin x}{x} \to 0 as x \to +\infty (bounded \sin, infinitesimal x resp. \frac1x), without computing anything.

Reciprocals: large and small

If \lvert f(x)\rvert \to +\infty as x \to x_0, then

\frac{1}{f(x)} \to 0.

Proof: Given \varepsilon > 0, choose K = 1/\varepsilon. For x sufficiently near x_0,

\lvert f(x)\rvert > K \implies \left\lvert \frac{1}{f(x)} \right\rvert < \frac1K = \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • K = \frac1\varepsilon — the size bound from the definition of "infinitely large", chosen so that its reciprocal is \varepsilon

The converse requires care: 1/f(x) \to 0 implies \lvert f(x)\rvert \to +\infty, provided f(x) is defined and nonzero near x_0.

Intuition

Shorthand for the two directions: "\frac{1}{\infty} = 0" and "\frac{1}{0} = \infty" — but the second only gives the size: \frac1x near 0 is infinitely large in magnitude, with sign - on the left and + on the right. To get +\infty or -\infty, look at the sign of the denominator on each side.

Cauchy criterion for a function limit

Theorem. f : D \to \mathbb{R} has a finite limit at x_0 if and only if

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0 : \quad \forall x, y \in D \cap \dot U(x_0, \delta), \quad \lvert f(x) - f(y)\rvert < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • x, y — any two inputs in the domain, both in the punctured \delta-neighbourhood of x_0
  • \lvert f(x) - f(y)\rvert — how far two function values near x_0 are from each other; no candidate limit appears

We compare any two function values close to x_0, without first knowing the candidate limit. This is the function version of the Cauchy criterion for sequences.

Connection

7 Limits of Sequences › The Cauchy convergence criterion: "late terms close to each other ⇔ convergent". Here "late" becomes "close to x_0". The "⇒" direction is the triangle inequality (\lvert f(x) - f(y)\rvert \le \lvert f(x) - a\rvert + \lvert a - f(y)\rvert < 2\cdot\frac\varepsilon2); the "⇐" direction uses completeness of \mathbb{R}, via Heine and the sequence criterion.

Using the Cauchy criterion to rule out a limit

Consider again f(x) = \sin(1/x) near 0.

x_n = \frac{1}{n\pi}, \qquad y_n = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/2}, \qquad x_n, y_n \to 0.

But

\lvert f(x_n) - f(y_n)\rvert = \lvert 0 - 1\rvert = 1 \quad \text{for every } n.
Symbols
  • x_n, y_n — the same two sequences as in Proving non-existence with two sequences

For \varepsilon_0 = \frac12, no punctured neighbourhood of 0 can make all values of f differ by less than \varepsilon_0.

Therefore the Cauchy criterion fails, so \lim_{x \to 0} \sin(1/x) does not exist.

Intuition

Three proofs of the same fact now stand side by side: two sequences with different image limits (Heine), a contradiction with a candidate a (\varepsilon–\delta), and two nearby points whose values stay 1 apart (Cauchy). The Cauchy version is the cleanest when no candidate a is in sight: inside every window around x_0, find two points whose values differ by a fixed amount.

One-sided limits

For a function defined to the right of x_0,

\lim_{x \to x_0^+} f(x) = a

means that f(x) approaches a as x approaches x_0 from above.

Right-hand limit:

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0 : \quad x \in D,\ x_0 < x < x_0 + \delta \implies \lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon.

The left-hand limit \lim_{x \to x_0^-} f(x) = b is defined similarly with x_0 - \delta < x < x_0.

Symbols
  • x \to x_0^+ — x tends to x_0 with x > x_0 (from the right / from above); x \to x_0^- — with x < x_0 (from the left / from below)
  • a — the right-hand limit, b — the left-hand limit
  • x_0 < x < x_0 + \delta — the right half of the punctured neighbourhood
Intuition

A one-sided limit is the ordinary limit of f restricted to one side: \lim_{x \to x_0^+} f(x) is the limit at x_0 of f on the smaller domain D \cap (x_0, \infty). So all the laws above (sums, products, squeeze, Heine with sequences x_n \downarrow x_0) hold for one-sided limits too.

A jump: left-hand and right-hand limits

Let

f(x) = \begin{cases} -1, & x < 0, \\ 1, & x \ge 0. \end{cases}

The step function: value -1 on the left (open circle at 0), value 1 from 0 on (filled dot at 0).

\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = -1, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = 1.

The two values differ, so there is no two-sided limit at 0.

Symbols
  • a piecewise-defined function (5 Functions › Piecewise-defined functions); f(0) = 1 (the filled dot), which plays no role in either one-sided limit

Practice: Khan Academy – one-sided limits from graphs (linked on slide 40).

When does a two-sided limit exist?

Theorem. A function f(x) has a limit as x approaches x_0 if and only if it has left-hand and right-hand limits there and these one-sided limits are equal:

\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = a \iff \lim_{x \to x_0^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to x_0^+} f(x) = a.
Symbols
  • a — the common value; the theorem assumes f is defined on both sides of x_0 (points of D arbitrarily close on the left and on the right)

Two common situations:

  • f(x) = \lvert x\rvert / x for x \neq 0: one-sided limits are -1 and 1.
  • f(x) = 1/x for x \neq 0: one-sided infinite limits are -\infty and +\infty.

When the domain approaches x_0 only from one side, the ordinary relative-to-domain limit is determined by that side.

Why do equal one-sided limits give the two-sided limit?

Given \varepsilon > 0, the left-hand limit gives some \delta_1 that works for x_0 - \delta_1 < x < x_0, and the right-hand limit some \delta_2 for x_0 < x < x_0 + \delta_2. With \delta = \min\{\delta_1, \delta_2\}, every x with 0 < \lvert x - x_0\rvert < \delta lies on one of the two sides and satisfies \lvert f(x) - a\rvert < \varepsilon. Conversely, a two-sided \delta works in particular on each side. Last sentence of the slide: for \sqrt{x} on D = [0, \infty), only right-hand points exist near 0, so \lim_{x \to 0} \sqrt x (relative to D) is just the right-hand limit, 0.

Quick check: do the one-sided limits agree?

Question: For

f(x) = \begin{cases} 2 + x, & x < 0, \\ -1 + x, & x \ge 0, \end{cases}

determine both one-sided limits at 0. Does the two-sided limit exist?

\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = 2, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = -1.

The one-sided limits are different. Hence \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) does not exist.

Symbols
  • each one-sided limit uses only the formula of its own side: 2 + x \to 2 from the left, -1 + x \to -1 from the right

More questions: Khan Academy – one-sided limits (linked on slide 42).

Worked example — absolute values hide two one-sided limits

Find \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^2 + x}{\lvert x\rvert}.

  1. Split by the sign of x: for x > 0, \lvert x\rvert = x; for x < 0, \lvert x\rvert = -x.
  2. Right-hand limit: \frac{x(x + 1)}{x} = x + 1 \to 1.
  3. Left-hand limit: \frac{x(x+1)}{-x} = -(x + 1) \to -1.
  4. Compare: 1 \neq -1, so the two-sided limit does not exist. (Checked numerically.) Signal to look for: \lvert\cdot\rvert, piecewise definitions, \sqrt{\ } at the edge of its domain, or \frac{1}{x - x_0} — each is a reason to compute the two sides separately.

Limits of monotonic functions

Increasing and decreasing functions

Let f : D \to \mathbb{R}. For any x_1, x_2 \in D with x_1 < x_2:

Increasing (non-decreasing)

f(x_1) \le f(x_2).

Decreasing (non-increasing)

f(x_1) \ge f(x_2).

Pictures on the slide: a rising line with f(x_1) below f(x_2), and a falling line with f(x_1) above f(x_2).

If the inequalities are strict for every x_1 < x_2, the function is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.

Symbols
  • x_1 < x_2 — any two points of the domain, in increasing order
  • in this lecture "increasing" means non-decreasing (\le); "strictly" adds <
Connection

Recap of 5 Functions › Increasing and decreasing functions, and the function version of monotone sequences (6 Sequences › Monotonicity of a sequence).

Limits of monotonic functions

Theorem. Let f : D \to \mathbb{R} be increasing. Suppose

\alpha = \inf D, \qquad \beta = \sup D, \qquad -\infty < \alpha < \beta < +\infty, \qquad \alpha, \beta \notin D.

Then f has one-sided limits at the endpoints (possibly infinite):

\lim_{x \to \alpha^+} f(x) = \inf_{x \in D} f(x), \qquad \lim_{x \to \beta^-} f(x) = \sup_{x \in D} f(x).
Symbols
  • \alpha = \inf D, \beta = \sup D — the left and right ends of the domain (3 Set of Real Numbers › Supremum and infimum); here \alpha, \beta are endpoints, not infinitesimals
  • \inf_{x \in D} f(x), \sup_{x \in D} f(x) — the infimum and supremum of all values of f; they may be -\infty resp. +\infty if f is unbounded

Example: D = (0, 1) and f(x) = \dfrac{x}{1+x} (strictly increasing).

\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = \frac12.

For a decreasing function, interchange inf and sup. If f is bounded on D, both limits are finite.

Why does the right-end limit equal the supremum?

Let s = \sup_{x \in D} f(x), assume it is finite, and let \varepsilon > 0. By the definition of supremum, some x_1 \in D has f(x_1) > s - \varepsilon. Set \delta = \beta - x_1 > 0. For every x \in D with \beta - \delta < x < \beta, i.e. x > x_1, monotonicity gives s - \varepsilon < f(x_1) \le f(x) \le s. So \lvert f(x) - s\rvert < \varepsilon. If s = +\infty, the same argument with "f(x_1) > K" gives the limit +\infty. This is exactly the proof of 7 Limits of Sequences › The monotone convergence theorem, with the index n replaced by x \to \beta^-.

Monotonicity gives endpoint limits

Example: f(x) = \dfrac{x}{1+x} for x > 0.

Graph on the slide: the curve rising from 0 at x = 0 towards the dashed line y = 1.

For 0 < x < y,

\frac{x}{1+x} < \frac{y}{1+y}.

Also 0 < f(x) < 1.

\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = 1.
Symbols
  • x, y — two inputs with 0 < x < y (here y is an input, not the vertical coordinate)
  • 0 and 1 — \inf f and \sup f over (0, \infty); neither is attained
Intuition

The monotonicity check: \frac{x}{1+x} = 1 - \frac{1}{1+x}, and \frac{1}{1+x} decreases as x grows. This rewriting also shows the two limits directly. Note that this example uses the right end \beta = +\infty, which the theorem on the previous slide excluded (\beta < +\infty); the same supremum argument works with "x > M" in place of "\beta - \delta < x", so the theorem extends to infinite endpoints.

Two special limits

The following limits are fundamental for later calculations:

A trigonometric limit

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1.

Angles must be measured in radians.

The number e

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \left(1 + \frac1x\right)^x = e, \qquad e \approx 2.71828.
Symbols
  • x — in the first limit an angle in radians, tending to 0; in the second a real number tending to +\infty
  • e — Euler's number (7 Limits of Sequences › Euler's number from a sequence)

We have already met the corresponding sequence limits. Here the variable x can take real values.

Practice: Khan Academy – determining trigonometric limits (linked on slide 46).

Common mistake — degrees

In degrees, \sin x^\circ = \sin\frac{\pi x}{180}, so \frac{\sin x^\circ}{x} \to \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745, not 1. Every formula derived from \frac{\sin x}{x} \to 1 (and later (\sin x)' = \cos x) silently assumes radians.

Why does the real-variable limit \left(1 + \frac1x\right)^x \to e follow from the sequence limit?

For x \ge 1 let n = \lfloor x\rfloor, so n \le x < n + 1. Then 1 + \frac{1}{n+1} < 1 + \frac1x \le 1 + \frac1n, and raising to powers between n and n + 1 gives \left(1 + \frac{1}{n+1}\right)^{n} \le \left(1 + \frac1x\right)^x \le \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^{n+1}. Both bounds tend to e as n \to \infty: the left one is \left(1 + \frac{1}{n+1}\right)^{n+1} / \left(1 + \frac{1}{n+1}\right), the right one is \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n \cdot \left(1 + \frac1n\right), and the extra factors tend to 1. The squeeze theorem finishes it.

Why \sin x / x \to 1?

For 0 < x < \pi/2, a standard geometric comparison gives

\sin x < x < \tan x.

Dividing by x and rearranging,

\cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x} < 1.

Since \lim_{x \to 0} \cos x = 1, the squeeze theorem implies

\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1.

Because (\sin x)/x is even, the two-sided limit is also 1. This argument assumes angles in radians; the geometry behind \sin x < x < \tan x is based on unit-circle areas.

Symbols
  • x \in (0, \frac\pi2) — an angle in radians in the first quadrant, where \sin x, \cos x, \tan x > 0
  • "even" — g(-x) = g(x) (5 Functions › Even and odd functions: symmetry): \frac{\sin(-x)}{-x} = \frac{-\sin x}{-x} = \frac{\sin x}{x}
Where do \sin x < x < \tan x and the rearrangement come from?

On the unit circle with angle x, compare three areas: the triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (\cos x, \sin x) has area \frac12\sin x; the circular sector has area \frac12 x (area \frac12 r^2 x with r = 1, radians!); the larger triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (1, \tan x) has area \frac12\tan x. Each region contains the previous one, so \frac12\sin x < \frac12 x < \frac12 \tan x. Rearranging: from \sin x < x, dividing by x > 0: \frac{\sin x}{x} < 1. From x < \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}, multiplying by \frac{\cos x}{x} > 0: \cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x}.

Useful trigonometric consequences

From \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1 we obtain

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(ax)}{\sin(bx)} = \frac{a}{b} \qquad (b \neq 0).

Also

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan x}{x} = 1, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\arcsin x}{x} = 1.

For the first formula, write \sin(ax)/\sin(bx) = (a/b)\,[\sin(ax)/(ax)]\,/\,[\sin(bx)/(bx)] when a \neq 0. The case a = 0 is immediate.

Symbols
  • a, b — real constants, b \neq 0 so the denominator \sin(bx) is not identically 0
  • \arcsin — the inverse of \sin on [-\frac\pi2, \frac\pi2] (5 Functions › Inverse trigonometric functions)
Why do \frac{\tan x}{x} and \frac{\arcsin x}{x} tend to 1?

\frac{\tan x}{x} = \frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos x} \to 1 \cdot 1 (product law). For \arcsin: substitute t = \arcsin x, so x = \sin t and t \to 0 as x \to 0 (and t \neq 0 for x \neq 0). Then \frac{\arcsin x}{x} = \frac{t}{\sin t} = 1 / \frac{\sin t}{t} \to 1. The substitution step — replace an inner expression by a new variable that also tends to 0 — is used in every example below.

Useful exponential consequences

\lim_{x \to 0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x} = 1, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1 + x)}{x} = 1,
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a^x - 1}{x \ln a} = 1 \quad (a > 0,\ a \neq 1), \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(1 + x)^\alpha - 1}{\alpha x} = 1 \quad (\alpha \neq 0).

For a, b \in \mathbb{R},

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \left(1 + \frac{a}{x}\right)^{bx} = e^{ab}.
Symbols
  • \ln — the natural logarithm (base e); a^x = e^{x \ln a} for a > 0
  • \alpha — a fixed real exponent, \alpha \neq 0 (not an infinitesimal here)
  • a, b — real constants in the last formula (a different a from the base a above)
How do these follow from (1 + \frac1x)^x \to e?
  • (1 + x)^{1/x}: put t = \frac1x; as x \to 0^+, t \to +\infty and the expression is \left(1 + \frac1t\right)^t \to e (the left side x \to 0^- uses the matching limit at -\infty).
  • \frac{\ln(1+x)}{x} = \ln\left((1+x)^{1/x}\right) \to \ln e = 1, since \ln can be swapped with the limit (continuity, next lecture).
  • \frac{e^x - 1}{x}: put t = e^x - 1 \to 0, so x = \ln(1 + t) and the quotient is \frac{t}{\ln(1+t)} \to 1.
  • \frac{a^x - 1}{x\ln a}: with u = x\ln a \to 0, it is \frac{e^u - 1}{u} \to 1.
  • \left(1 + \frac ax\right)^{bx} with a \neq 0: put t = \frac xa; then it is \left(\left(1 + \frac1t\right)^t\right)^{ab} \to e^{ab} (for a < 0, t \to -\infty). For a = 0 both sides are 1.
Intuition — the pattern behind all of them

Each formula says that near x = 0 some function behaves like a straight line through the origin: \sin x \approx x, \tan x \approx x, e^x - 1 \approx x, \ln(1 + x) \approx x, (1+x)^\alpha - 1 \approx \alpha x. Replacing these by their linear approximations is a reliable way to guess a limit; the formulas then prove it. (These are the derivatives at 0 in disguise — next lectures.)

Some further useful limits

Reciprocal limits

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac1x = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac1x = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac1x = +\infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac1x = -\infty.

Exponential decay or growth

\lim_{x \to +\infty} a^{-x} = \begin{cases} 0, & a > 1, \\ 1, & a = 1, \\ +\infty, & 0 < a < 1. \end{cases}

Even very slowly growing functions can be unbounded:

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \sqrt[x]{x} = \lim_{x \to +\infty} x^{1/x} = 1.
Symbols
  • a > 0 — the base; a^{-x} = \left(\frac1a\right)^x decays if a > 1 and grows if 0 < a < 1
  • \sqrt[x]{x} = x^{1/x} = e^{\ln x / x} — the "x-th root of x" for real x > 0

Why is x^{1/x} \to 1?

Write x^{1/x} = e^{\ln x / x}. The exponent \frac{\ln x}{x} \to 0 as x \to +\infty (the logarithm grows more slowly than any positive power of x; for integers this is the comparison behind \sqrt[n]{n} \to 1 in 7 Limits of Sequences › Common limits: n-th root), so x^{1/x} \to e^0 = 1. Numerically: 1000^{1/1000} \approx 1.0069.

Worked examples from the lecture

Example: \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos x - 1}{x}

Use \cos x = 1 - 2\sin^2(x/2):

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos x - 1}{x} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-2\sin^2(x/2)}{x} = -\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\,\sin(x/2).

Set t = x/2, so that t \to 0. Then

= -\underbrace{\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin t}{t}}_{1}\ \underbrace{\lim_{t \to 0} \sin t}_{0} = 0.
Symbols
  • \cos x = 1 - 2\sin^2\frac x2 — the half-angle (double-angle) identity (5 Functions › Useful identities: trigonometry)
  • \frac{-2\sin^2(x/2)}{x} = -\frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\sin\frac x2 — since \frac{2}{x} = \frac{1}{x/2}
  • t = \frac x2 — the substitution; t \to 0 exactly when x \to 0

Example: \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(2x)}{5x}

Factor out the constant:

\frac{\sin(2x)}{5x} = \frac25 \cdot \frac{\sin(2x)}{2x}.

Now substitute t = 2x, so t \to 0:

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(2x)}{5x} = \frac25 \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin t}{t} = \frac25.
Symbols
  • t = 2x — chosen to match the argument of the sine, so that \frac{\sin t}{t} appears

Example: \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan x \sec(2x)}{3x}

Recall \tan x = \sin x / \cos x and \sec(2x) = 1/\cos(2x).

\frac{\tan x \sec(2x)}{3x} = \frac13 \cdot \frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos x} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos(2x)}.

All factors have finite limits:

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan x \sec(2x)}{3x} = \frac13 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = \frac13.
Symbols
  • \sec y = \frac{1}{\cos y} — the secant; \cos x \to 1 and \cos(2x) \to 1 as x \to 0

Example: a composite trigonometric limit

Evaluate

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(2x^3 + 3x)}{5x - x^5}.

Write the quotient as

\frac{\sin(2x^3 + 3x)}{5x - x^5} = \underbrace{\frac{\sin(2x^3 + 3x)}{2x^3 + 3x}}_{\to 1} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{2x^2 + 3}{5 - x^4}}_{\to 3/5}.
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(2x^3 + 3x)}{5x - x^5} = \frac35.
Symbols
  • first factor: \frac{\sin u}{u} with u = 2x^3 + 3x \to 0 (and u \neq 0 for small x \neq 0)
  • second factor: \frac{2x^3 + 3x}{5x - x^5} = \frac{x(2x^2 + 3)}{x(5 - x^4)}, cancelled by x \neq 0, then direct substitution

Example: a quotient of trigonometric factors

Calculate

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos(3x)}{\tan(2x)\sin(4x)}.

Use 1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2(t/2), then

\begin{aligned} \frac{1 - \cos(3x)}{\tan(2x)\sin(4x)} &= \frac{2\sin^2(3x/2)}{\tan(2x)\sin(4x)} \\ &= \frac{(3x)^2}{(2x)(4x)} \cdot \frac12 \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{\sin(3x/2)}{3x/2}\right)^2}_{\to 1} \underbrace{\frac{2x}{\tan(2x)}}_{\to 1} \underbrace{\frac{4x}{\sin(4x)}}_{\to 1}. \end{aligned}
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos(3x)}{\tan(2x)\sin(4x)} = \frac{9}{16}.
Symbols
  • 1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2\frac t2 with t = 3x
  • \frac{(3x)^2}{(2x)(4x)} = \frac{9x^2}{8x^2} = \frac98, times \frac12 gives \frac{9}{16}
Why is the second line equal to the first?

Multiply out the constants and powers of x in the second line: \frac{9x^2}{8x^2} \cdot \frac12 \cdot \frac{\sin^2(3x/2)}{9x^2/4} \cdot \frac{2x \cdot 4x}{\tan(2x)\sin(4x)} = \frac{9}{16} \cdot \frac{4}{9x^2} \cdot 8x^2 \cdot \frac{\sin^2(3x/2)}{\tan(2x)\sin(4x)} = 2 \cdot \frac{\sin^2(3x/2)}{\tan(2x)\sin(4x)}, which is the first line. The trick: every trigonometric factor is paired with its own argument (\frac{\sin u}{u}, \frac{v}{\tan v}, …), and the arguments that were "borrowed" are paid back in the rational prefactor \frac{(3x)^2}{(2x)(4x)}. (The value \frac{9}{16} was checked numerically.)

Quick check: a trigonometric limit

Question: Evaluate

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(3x)}{2x}.

Separate a familiar limit:

\frac{\sin(3x)}{2x} = \frac32 \cdot \frac{\sin(3x)}{3x}.

With u = 3x \to 0 and \sin u / u \to 1,

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(3x)}{2x} = \frac32.
Symbols
  • u = 3x — the substitution matching the sine's argument

Worked example — the recipe for trigonometric \frac00 limits

Find \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(5x)}{\tan(3x)} and \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2}.

  1. Pair each trig factor with its argument: \frac{\sin(5x)}{\tan(3x)} = \frac{\sin(5x)}{5x} \cdot \frac{3x}{\tan(3x)} \cdot \frac{5x}{3x}.
  2. Each pair tends to 1, the leftover is rational: limit = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \frac53 = \frac53.
  3. For 1 - \cos, first convert to \sin^2: \frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2} = \frac12\left(\frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2 \to \frac12. (Both checked numerically.) Compare with the lecture's \frac{\cos x - 1}{x} \to 0: dividing by x^2 instead of x leaves a non-zero limit, because 1 - \cos x is about \frac{x^2}{2} near 0.
Common mistake — "\frac{\sin(3x)}{2x} = \frac{\sin 3}{2}" or "\sin cancels"

\sin(3x) is not \sin 3 \cdot x, and \frac{\sin(ax)}{\sin(bx)} is not \frac ab by cancelling "sin" — it equals \frac ab only in the limit x \to 0, by the special limit. At x = 1, \frac{\sin 3}{\sin 2} \approx 0.155, nowhere near \frac32. The argument of \frac{\sin u}{u} must match exactly and must tend to 0: \frac{\sin x}{x} \to 0 as x \to +\infty, not 1.

Example: a limit of the form (1 + c/x)^{x+d}

Find

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \left(1 - \frac{2}{3x}\right)^{x+3}.

Set t = -3x/2, so t \to -\infty and

1 - \frac{2}{3x} = 1 + \frac1t, \qquad x + 3 = -\frac23 t + 3.

Thus

\left(1 - \frac{2}{3x}\right)^{x+3} = \left(\left(1 + \frac1t\right)^t\right)^{-2/3 + 3/t} \longrightarrow e^{-2/3}.
Symbols
  • t = -\frac{3x}{2} — chosen so that -\frac{2}{3x} = \frac1t; then x = -\frac{2t}{3}
  • the exponent: t \cdot \left(-\frac23 + \frac3t\right) = -\frac{2t}{3} + 3 = x + 3
  • \left(1 + \frac1t\right)^t \to e also as t \to -\infty (the slides use this without stating it separately)
Why does the last step give e^{-2/3}?

The inner part \left(1 + \frac1t\right)^t \to e and the outer exponent -\frac23 + \frac3t \to -\frac23. A power with a positive base and both base and exponent converging behaves well: u(t)^{v(t)} = e^{v(t)\ln u(t)} \to e^{-\frac23 \ln e} = e^{-2/3} \approx 0.513. The same answer comes from the general formula \left(1 + \frac ax\right)^{bx} \to e^{ab} with a = -\frac23, b = 1; the extra "+3" in the exponent contributes the factor \left(1 - \frac{2}{3x}\right)^3 \to 1. (Checked numerically: at x = 10^7 the value is 0.51342.)

Example: a rational expression raised to x

Evaluate

\lim_{x \to +\infty} \left(\frac{x^3 + 2x^2 + 1}{x^3 + x - 7}\right)^x.

Rewrite the base:

\frac{x^3 + 2x^2 + 1}{x^3 + x - 7} = 1 + \frac{2x^2 - x + 8}{x^3 + x - 7}.

Set u(x) = \dfrac{2x^2 - x + 8}{x^3 + x - 7}. Then u(x) \to 0 and

x\,u(x) = \frac{2 - 1/x + 8/x^2}{1 + 1/x^2 - 7/x^3} \longrightarrow 2.

Therefore

\lim_{x \to +\infty} (1 + u(x))^x = e^2.
Symbols
  • u(x) — the part of the base beyond 1: numerator minus denominator, over the denominator; u(x) \to 0 since its degree difference is 2 - 3 < 0
  • x\,u(x) — the exponent times the excess; it decides the answer e^{\lim x u(x)}
Why does (1 + u(x))^x tend to e^{\lim x\,u(x)}?

Write (1 + u(x))^x = \left((1 + u(x))^{1/u(x)}\right)^{x\,u(x)} (valid where u(x) \neq 0, which holds for large x since u(x) > 0 there). As u(x) \to 0, the inner bracket tends to e (the formula (1 + t)^{1/t} \to e as t \to 0 from Useful exponential consequences), and the exponent x\,u(x) \to 2. So the whole expression tends to e^2 \approx 7.389 (numerically checked).

Worked example — the "1^\infty" recipe

(a) \displaystyle\lim_{x \to +\infty} \left(1 + \frac3x\right)^{2x}: formula \left(1 + \frac ax\right)^{bx} \to e^{ab} with a = 3, b = 2: e^6. (b) \displaystyle\lim_{x \to +\infty} \left(\frac{x + 1}{x - 2}\right)^x.

  1. Check the form: base \to 1, exponent \to \infty: "1^\infty", indeterminate.
  2. Write the base as 1 + u: \frac{x+1}{x-2} = 1 + \frac{3}{x - 2}, so u(x) = \frac{3}{x-2} \to 0.
  3. Compute exponent × excess: x\,u(x) = \frac{3x}{x - 2} \to 3.
  4. Conclude: limit = e^3 \approx 20.09. (Both checked numerically.)
Common mistake — "1^\infty = 1"

The base tends to 1, and 1 to any power is 1, so the answer "must be 1"? No: the base is only close to 1, and a huge exponent amplifies the small excess. \left(1 + \frac1x\right)^x \to e, \left(1 + \frac1x\right)^{x^2} \to +\infty, \left(1 + \frac{1}{x^2}\right)^x \to 1: everything depends on exponent × excess. "1^\infty" is an indeterminate form, like \frac00.

AreaWhere limits appear

Intuition — a steady value is a horizontal asymptote

A typical response of a controlled system to a step command is y(t) = 1 - e^{-t/\tau} (\tau > 0 a time constant). By Some further useful limits, e^{-t/\tau} \to 0 as t \to +\infty, so y(t) \to 1: the system settles at the commanded value, and y = 1 is a horizontal asymptote of the response. "Steady-state value" in control is exactly \lim_{t \to +\infty} y(t).
